# Literature Review {#sec-lit-review}

This chapter reviews the methodological foundations that motivate the rest of the thesis, beginning with the design and analysis of cluster-randomized trials and then turning to related topics such as the intraclass correlation coefficient, missing data, and multiple imputation.

## Cluster Randomized Trials {#sec-crt}

In health and social science research, studies often randomize entire pre-existing groups---such as clinics, schools, or communities---instead of single individuals. As @lorenzClusterRandomizedStudies2018a and @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 explain, this approach is essential when an intervention naturally targets a whole environment or to prevent "contamination," which occurs when control group members accidentally adopt aspects of the treatment from their peers. These studies can take several structural forms, including classic CRTs, stepped-wedge designs (where groups cross over to the intervention sequentially over time), and partially clustered trials (where individuals are randomized independently but receive treatment in group settings). Regardless of the specific design, grouping participants fundamentally changes how we view statistical data: people in the same cluster share identical staff, environments, and policies, making their outcomes naturally more alike. While statistical models can account for this group structure, they cannot eliminate or mitigate the underlying lack of independence among individuals---it remains an inherent feature of the data.

To measure this group similarity, researchers calculate the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC). The ICC is then used to determine the "design effect," a scaling formula that illustrates how the impact of correlation is strongly magnified by cluster sample size. Accounting for the design effect is essential in both the planning and analysis phases of a study: failing to use it during sample size design leads to underpowered trials and high Type II error rates (false negatives), while ignoring it during final analysis understates uncertainty and inflates Type I error rates (false positives).

Specifically, because outcomes within groups are linked, analyzing cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) requires statistical models that directly account for this correlation structure. @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 trace how analytical methods have evolved over time---moving from simple cluster-level summaries to individual-level approaches like linear mixed models and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). They emphasize that no single analysis method is universally superior because each involves distinct statistical trade-offs. For instance, @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 note that while collapsing data into a single cluster summary score is simple and avoids complex statistical modeling, it cannot easily adjust for individual participant traits (like age or baseline health status). Building smoothly on these analytical choices, @billotHowShouldCluster2024 explain why individual-level regression methods are generally preferred in trial practice. Beyond allowing researchers to adjust for baseline participant traits to improve estimation precision, individual-level mixed-effects models explicitly separate between-cluster variance from within-cluster variance, providing the exact model components needed to calculate the ICC directly.

However, analyzing CRTs becomes significantly more complex when trials face real-world complications like missing data and small sample sizes. @billotHowShouldCluster2024 point out that simply accounting for clustering in a model does not solve the challenge of missing participant outcomes, which requires deliberate imputation strategies. Compounding this difficulty, @kahanIncreasedRiskType2016 demonstrate that standard, uncorrected mixed models and GEE tend to underestimate standard errors when cluster counts are low (frequently under 30 to 70 clusters). This distortion creates a high risk of Type I errors---or false positives---tricking researchers into declaring a treatment effective when it is not, with false-positive rates often soaring far above the standard 5% target. To prevent misleading conclusions, @kahanIncreasedRiskType2016 highlight the necessity of applying small-sample corrections (such as Satterthwaite degree-of-freedom adjustments or Fay-Graubard variance corrections) to restore proper standard errors.

Together, these foundational articles reveal how clustering affects every stage of research, from initial sample size planning to final statistical modeling. Ignoring intra-cluster correlation artificially inflates statistical power and understates uncertainty. Understanding these basic CRT mechanics provides a strong foundation for exploring how downstream complications---specifically missing data and ICC estimation---must be handled without destroying the underlying group structure.

## Intracluster Correlation Coefficient {#sec-icc}

In cluster randomized trials (CRTs), individuals within the same cluster often have more similar outcomes because they share environments, healthcare providers, or other characteristics. This similarity is measured using the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC), which can be understood in two related ways. As @kerryIntraclusterCorrelationCoefficient1998a explain, ICC is both a measure of correlation and a proportion of variance. As a correlation, it measures how strongly the outcomes of two individuals from the same cluster are related. Under a simple random-intercept model, it also represents the proportion of total outcome variation that comes from differences between clusters rather than differences between individuals within clusters, $\operatorname{ICC} = \sigma^2_{\text{between}} / (\sigma^2_{\text{between}} + \sigma^2_{\text{within}})$. For example, an ICC of 0.10 means that 10% of the total variation is attributable to differences between clusters. These two interpretations are mathematically equivalent under this model because the correlation between two individuals in the same cluster is determined by the amount of variation they share at the cluster level.

Understanding ICC is particularly important when designing CRTs because individuals within the same cluster do not provide as much independent statistical information as individuals from different clusters. @kerryIntraclusterCorrelationCoefficient1998a demonstrate that even a small ICC can substantially increase the sample size needed to achieve adequate statistical power (the probability of detecting a true treatment effect). Researchers account for this using the design effect, $\operatorname{DE} = 1 + (m - 1) \times \operatorname{ICC}$, where $m$ is the number of individuals per cluster, which shows how the impact of correlation increases with cluster size. However, the true ICC is generally unknown when planning a study, so researchers must estimate it using existing clustered data or borrow estimates from previous studies. This makes the accuracy and reliability of ICC estimation particularly important.

A major challenge is that ICC estimates can be highly uncertain, particularly when studies contain relatively few clusters. @Ukoumunne2002 investigated this problem by comparing different methods for constructing confidence intervals (intervals designed to contain the true ICC at a specified rate across repeated studies). Using simulations and real trial data, the author found that some methods provided more reliable confidence intervals than others, but estimates were often imprecise, and violations of statistical assumptions could further reduce their reliability. Since even small changes in ICC can substantially affect sample size calculations, this uncertainty has important practical consequences. @campbellIntraclusterCorrelationCoefficients2004 further emphasize the importance of reporting ICC estimates alongside their confidence intervals, estimation methods, and study characteristics. Without this information, researchers may struggle to determine whether an ICC estimate from one study is appropriate for another.

Beyond estimation uncertainty, ICC values also depend on the outcome being measured, the population being studied, and the statistical model used to calculate them. @eldridgeIntraClusterCorrelationCoefficient2009 explain that ICCs can be defined and estimated differently for continuous outcomes (such as blood pressure) and binary outcomes (such as whether a patient develops a disease). Estimates may also change when researchers adjust for individual characteristics, such as age or baseline health status, because these variables can explain some of the differences between clusters. @pagelIntraclusterCorrelationCoefficients2011a demonstrate this variation using maternal and newborn health data from five CRTs, finding that mortality outcomes generally had much smaller ICCs than healthcare behavior outcomes. They also showed that rare outcomes, such as maternal mortality, could produce particularly unstable ICC estimates because relatively few events were observed. These findings show that ICC is not a universal characteristic of clustered data; its value and interpretation depend on the outcome, study setting, and estimation approach.

Together, these papers establish the main statistical foundations of ICC: what it measures, why it matters for CRT design, how it is estimated, and why its estimates may be uncertain or vary across studies. Although ICC provides a relatively simple measure of similarity within clusters, obtaining a reliable estimate is not always straightforward. Its precision depends on the number and size of clusters, the distribution and type of outcome, and the statistical assumptions used. Consequently, understanding ICC requires considering not only its estimated value but also how that value was obtained, how much uncertainty surrounds it, and whether it is appropriate for the study in which it will be used.
